segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding the key to the abyss and a great chain in his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and threw him into the abyss and shut and sealed it over him, so that he would no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years were completed. After this he must be released for a short time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw thrones, and those who sat on them were entrusted with judgment. And I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded because of the testimony of Jesus and because of the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received the mark on their foreheads or on their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were completed. This is the first resurrection.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no authority, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he will go out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for the war; their number is like the sand of the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the holy ones and the beloved city. And fire came down from heaven and consumed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the devil, who had been deceiving them, was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet also are, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw a great white throne and the one seated on it. From his presence earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw the dead, the great and the small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged from what was written in the books, according to their works.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, and Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one according to their works.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And anyone who was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire.

notes.note: The King James Version and several modern versions have “bottomless pit”, a rendering drawn from the word’s etymology. In the Septuagint the word names the primeval deep, and by the first century it was also used for the underworld where hostile spirits are confined (compare Luke 8:31). “Abyss”, which some modern translations also use, avoids suggesting a literal shaft without a floor.

This period is mentioned six times in verses 2–7 and nowhere else in the New Testament; it is the source of the word “millennium”. Interpreters have long disagreed on whether it is a future reign following Christ’s return, a symbolic figure for the present era between his first and second comings, or a future golden age before his return. The translation does not decide between these readings.

The Greek word is the same one rendered “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament. It means peoples or nations, and in Jewish usage often the non-Jewish peoples specifically. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so “nations” is used, as in most translations.

The Greek says literally that “judgment was given to them”. Most interpreters take this as authority to judge, and the rendering follows that view. It can also mean that a verdict was given in their favor, echoing Daniel 7:22. The Greek does not say who sits on the thrones.

notes.phrase: and those who had not worshiped the beast
notes.note: The Greek can be read as a further description of the beheaded martyrs or as adding a second, wider group: all who refused the beast, whether or not they were killed. The rendering leaves both readings open, as the Greek does.

The verb is the ordinary word “live”, and the form used here can mean either “they lived” (so the King James Version) or “they came to life”. Most modern translations choose the latter, as at Revelation 2:8, where the same form is used of Christ. Whether this means bodily resurrection or life with Christ after death is a long-standing dispute, tied to how the thousand years are understood.

notes.phrase: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were completed.
notes.note: This sentence is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and a number of later manuscripts, probably because a copyist’s eye skipped from one “thousand years” to the next. It is generally accepted as original. The sentence is an aside: “This is the first resurrection” refers back to the coming to life in verse 4.

Most translations have “power”. The Greek word denotes the right or jurisdiction to act, not raw strength, for which Greek has a different word. The point is that the second death has no claim on these people.

In Ezekiel 38–39 Gog, of the land of Magog, leads a great coalition of nations against Israel and is destroyed by God. Here the two names together stand for the hostile nations of the whole earth. Jewish tradition also came to treat the two names as a pair.

Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people”. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue.

notes.traditional: fire came down from God out of heaven
notes.note: Many later manuscripts read “from God out of heaven”, the reading behind the King James Version, and there are other variations in the wording. The shorter text has good early support and is preferred by modern critical editions.

A first-century reader would have pictured scrolls. The scene draws on Daniel 7:10, where the court sits and books are opened. The “books” are records of deeds, while the “book of life” is pictured as a register of names, like a city’s roll of citizens (compare Exodus 32:32 and Daniel 12:1).

candidates.reason: Translations split between “bottomless pit”, “Abyss” and “the deep” across Luke 8:31, Romans 10:7 and Revelation, and a reader should see that it is one place-term.
It recurs across the Gospels, the letters and Revelation, where “deceive”, “lead astray” and “go astray” are all defensible and varying them hides a thematic thread.
It is very frequent, and translations waver between “authority”, “power” and “right”, blurring the distinction from δύναμις.
Judgment “according to works” here and in Romans 2:6 should visibly connect with Paul’s and James’s “works” language, but translators vary between “works”, “deeds” and “what they had done”.
Translations switch between “scroll” (Revelation 5, Luke 4) and “book” (book of life, Revelation 22), and one policy is needed on when the scroll format should show in English.
